questions.prompt: Roughly how long should Keshav's first pass take?
questions.explanation: The first pass skims title, abstract, introduction, headings and conclusions in about 5 to 10 minutes; the third pass can take hours.

questions.prompt: Which section usually holds the settings needed to reproduce results?
questions.explanation: Skipping the limitations and appendix is a listed mistake; crucial settings often live there.

questions.prompt: Qualitative examples in a paper are illustrations, not evidence of general performance.
questions.explanation: True. They can be cherry-picked; look at the quantitative tables, variance and ablations.

questions.prompt: A paper compares its tuned method with baseline numbers copied from older papers. What should you check?
options: Whether conditions are matched: same data splits, compute budget, evaluation protocol and comparable tuning effort
questions.explanation: Copied numbers may use different splits or compute; matched conditions are essential.

questions.prompt: The abstract claims +3 points. The table shows a single run, no standard deviation, and seed variance elsewhere is about 2 points. How should you read it?
options: Weak evidence: one run with no variance; the gain may be within noise
questions.explanation: Ignoring variance mistakes noise for progress.

questions.prompt: Which are signs of possible benchmark contamination? Select all that apply.
options: Much higher scores on an old public benchmark than on fresh similar questions
The model can complete benchmark questions verbatim
n-gram overlap between training data and test items
Consistent scores on old and new sets
questions.explanation: Consistent performance on new items suggests real capability; the others suggest memorisation.

questions.prompt: A method introduces five changes at once and reports only the combined result. What is missing?
options: Ablations removing each component, so you know which changes cause the gain
questions.explanation: Without ablations you cannot tell what helped.

questions.prompt: You will reproduce a paper. What should you do first?
options: Reproduce the headline result first, using released code if available, recording environment, versions, seeds, hardware and deviations
questions.explanation: Start with the headline result; partial reproduction is still informative if documented.

questions.prompt: A paper uses an LLM judge as its main metric. What should you look for?
options: Whether the judge was validated against human labels and whether its model and prompt are pinned
questions.explanation: Unvalidated judges can be biased; check agreement with humans.

coding.title: n-gram contamination check
coding.prompt: Write `contamination(test_items, corpus, n=8, threshold=0.5)` that lowercases and splits text into words, builds the set of all word n-grams from `corpus` (a list of strings), and for each test item computes the fraction of its n-grams found in that set. Return the indexes of test items whose fraction is `>= threshold`. Items with fewer than n words have no n-grams and are never flagged.
coding.explanation: Long n-gram overlap between training data and test items is one of the standard contamination checks; long exact word sequences rarely match by chance, so high overlap suggests the item was in the training data.
hints: Write an n-gram helper returning tuples of n consecutive words.
Put every corpus n-gram in a set.

tests.name: Flags a copied item
tests.code:
corpus=['the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank today']
tests=['The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river','a completely different question about matrix shapes and gradients today']
assert contamination(tests,corpus,n=5)==[0], contamination(tests,corpus,n=5)

tests.name: Short items never flagged
tests.code:
assert contamination(['the quick'],['the quick brown'],n=3)==[]
assert contamination(['a b c'],['a b c'],n=3)==[0]
